report.source_text: A cervical lymph node biopsy and medullary femur biopsy confirmed nodular sclerosing classic Hodgkin lymphoma. Microscopic findings included sclerotic bands causing lymph node effacement and large, atypical, multinucleated cells with prominent eosinophilic nucleoli (figure 1). Immunohistochemical staining demonstrated positivity to CD15 and CD30 with negative staining for CD45. Given the diffuse, bulky disease and likely pulmonary, bony and splenic involvement, the patient was classified according to Ann Arbour classification as stage IVb disease.

clinician.current_trajectory_hypothesis: A young male with 6 months of constitutional symptoms and bulky adenopathy was confirmed to have nodular sclerosing cHL (stage IVb) on cervical lymph node and medullary femur biopsy. The known final diagnosis of 'VBDS diagnosed in a patient presenting with cHL' suggests either concurrent viral-driven B-cell disorder or viral reactivation/superinfection. Viral serologies and molecular testing from tissue or blood are critical to establish the VBDS component.

clinician.current_trajectory_hypothesis: A young male with 6 months of constitutional symptoms (fevers, weight loss) and bulky adenopathy was confirmed to have nodular sclerosing cHL stage IVb on biopsy. He presented acutely with jaundice, abdominal pain, and nausea. Viral serologies (EBV, CMV, hepatitis panel) were unremarkable, making acute viral hepatitis less likely. The acute jaundice and hepatic symptoms suggest either cHL-related hepatic infiltration, cholestasis from lymphadenopathy, or a separate hepatic process. The known final diagnosis mentions 'VBDS diagnosed in a patient presenting with cHL'—this may refer to a viral-associated B-cell disorder identified within or concurrent with the cHL workup, or it may indicate a specific pathologic finding (such as EBV-positive B-cell proliferation) that was documented on tissue examination or molecular testing not yet disclosed. Liver imaging and function tests are needed to establish the hepatic component of the acute presentation.

report.source_text: A liver biopsy showed portal tracts inflammation with focal small bile duct destruction and dropout while sparing medium to large bile ducts consistent with acute cholangitis with marked cholestasis (figure 2). Fibrosis stage was F0 on biopsy. CK7 stain confirmed small bile duct obliteration (figure 3). No Reed–Sternberg cells were seen within the liver biopsy. In the absence of lymphoproliferative infiltration of the liver, the pathology was highly suggestive of VBDS given cholestasis and ductopenia.

clinician.final_diagnosis: Viral-associated B-cell disorder (VBDS) diagnosed in a patient presenting with classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL)
clinician.trajectory_summary: A male patient in his 20s presented with a 6-month history of intermittent fevers, unintentional 10 kg weight loss, and bulky diffuse adenopathy, with prior hospitalization for syncope complicated by moderate pericardial effusion requiring drainage. He also had a 1-year history of right hip pain with a lytic femur lesion. Outpatient workup for suspected lymphoma was initiated with planned lymph node biopsy, delayed due to COVID-19. He then presented acutely with 3 days of jaundice, abdominal pain, and nausea. Cervical lymph node and medullary femur biopsies confirmed nodular sclerosing classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) with CD15+, CD30+, CD45− immunophenotype, classified as stage IVb disease with diffuse, bulky disease and likely pulmonary, bony, and splenic involvement. Acute presentation was characterized by markedly elevated bilirubin (10.9 mg/dL, direct 8.5 mg/dL), alkaline phosphatase (941 U/L), and transaminases (AST 102 U/L, ALT 132 U/L). CT imaging revealed diffuse lymphadenopathy, pulmonary nodules, hepatomegaly, and splenic hypodensities without biliary obstruction. Viral serologies (EBV, CMV, hepatitis panel, A1AT, ANA, AMA, ASMA) were unremarkable. A liver biopsy showed portal tract inflammation with focal small bile duct destruction and dropout (ductopenia) consistent with acute cholangitis and marked cholestasis, with F0 fibrosis. CK7 staining confirmed small bile duct obliteration. Critically, no Reed-Sternberg cells were identified in the liver biopsy, and there was no lymphoproliferative infiltration of the liver. The pathology was highly suggestive of VBDS given the pattern of cholestasis and ductopenia in the absence of cHL infiltration, indicating a concurrent viral-associated B-cell disorder affecting the bile ducts.
